contribution: Energy gets the unit joule and the prefixes kJ, MJ, GJ and TJ: conservation and transformation of energy are shown as chains in which part turns into heat at every step, and everyday and societal energies are compared by order of magnitude on a ladder.
learn: You can explain an energy chain and what the energy finally turns into.
You can give energy in joules and with the prefixes kJ, MJ, GJ and TJ.
You can compare everyday and societal energies by order of magnitude.
prior: Energy appears in different forms and is conserved (chapter *Forms of energy and conservation of energy*)
The prefixes kilo, mega, giga and tera are powers of ten (chapter *Quantities, units and the SI system*)
Powers of ten and orders of magnitude (chapter *Physics as a science and the scales of the universe*)

activities.text: In the morning you eat oat porridge and set off to school by bike. The pedals turn, your speed stays up and the tyres warm up. When you arrive, you brake and stop. The oats grew in a field through the summer, and the Sun shone on them the whole time.
activities.question: Where does the energy of the bicycle's motion come from, and where does it finally go when you stop?

activities.title: Review: conservation of energy
activities.prompt: A car brakes and stops. Which description of its kinetic energy is correct (chapter *Forms of energy and conservation of energy*)?

choices.text: The kinetic energy disappears, because the car is no longer moving.
choices.feedback: Energy does not disappear. When the car stops, its kinetic energy turns into other energy, and there is as much energy in total as before braking.

choices.text: The kinetic energy turns mostly into thermal energy in the brakes, tyres and road, and there is as much energy in total as before.
choices.feedback: Correct. Energy is conserved and changes form: kinetic energy becomes heat, which spreads into the surroundings. Today we examine such chains and calculate energy in joules.

choices.text: The kinetic energy is transferred to the road and stays there as kinetic energy.
choices.feedback: The road does not start moving, so the energy does not stay there as kinetic energy. It turns into thermal energy, which warms the brakes, tyres and road.

activities.title: Prediction 1: petrol or food
activities.prompt: Which contains more chemical energy: one litre of petrol or an adult's food for a whole day?

choices.text: A day's food, because it gives a person the strength to be active all day.
choices.feedback: The table values refute this: a day's food is about $10\,\text{MJ}$ and a litre of petrol about $32\,\text{MJ}$. Being able to keep going does not show how much energy there is, because the body turns a large part of the energy of food into heat.

choices.text: A litre of petrol, about three times as much.
choices.feedback: The values support this: a litre of petrol is about $32\,\text{MJ}$ and a day's food about $10\,\text{MJ}$, so the ratio is $32\,\text{MJ} : 10\,\text{MJ} \approx 3.2$. A small amount of fuel contains a lot of energy.

choices.text: The same, because you can travel about the same distance with either.
choices.feedback: The values refute this: $32\,\text{MJ}$ and $10\,\text{MJ}$. Distance does not show how much energy there is, because a large part of the energy of fuel turns into heat in the engine of the car.

activities.title: Prediction 2: the Sun and humankind
activities.prompt: The Sun sends radiation energy to the Earth all the time. Its radiation warms the whole planet and keeps up the winds, the rains and the growth of plants, whereas human power plants and engines are small dots on the surface of the Earth. How long does it take for the total energy use of humankind (electricity, heating, transport, industry) to equal one hour of solar radiation reaching the Earth?

choices.feedback: The values refute this: an hour of solar radiation reaching the Earth is about $6.2 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{J}$, and in 2023 humankind used about $6.2 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{J}$ in a whole year.

The values support this: the Sun delivers about $6.2 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{J}$ in an hour, and the energy use of humankind in a year was about $6.2 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{J}$, that is, of the same order of magnitude.

The values refute this: in a thousand years humankind would use about a thousand times as much, $6 \cdot 10^{23}\,\text{J}$. That much solar radiation reaches the Earth in about a thousand hours, that is, about $40$ days, not in one hour.

activities.text: Each step on the ladder is a factor of ten. Choose an item and see which step it falls on.
activities.howto: Choose an energy from the *Item* menu, and the view moves to it; the energy of the chosen item is shown under its name. With the buttons you move up or down the ladder, and one press is one power of ten. A filled dot means a value from a source or a calculation, a ring means an estimate. The value and source of the chosen item are also shown below the ladder.
activities.model: The values are rounded orders of magnitude, not exact measurements: the energy of a lightning strike varies a lot, and the energy of a day's food depends on the person. Each item has a source (a table value, a statistic or a calculation) or is marked as an estimate. The scale is logarithmic, so the same distance on the ladder always means the same number of times more energy.
activities.calc: The energy of each item is written as a number times a power of ten, for example $3.2 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{J}$. The prefix is obtained by replacing the power with its value: $10^{6}\,\text{J} = 1\,\text{MJ}$, so $3.2 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{J} = 32 \cdot 10^{6}\,\text{J} = 32\,\text{MJ}$. When two items are compared, the larger energy is divided by the smaller: $32\,\text{MJ} : 10\,\text{MJ} = 3.2$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: petrol and food
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. In the *Item* menu, select first a day's food and then a litre of petrol, and record the energy of each in megajoules. You can also record a banana and a chocolate bar.

activities.title: Experiment 2: the Sun and humankind
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. In the *Item* menu, select first the solar radiation reaching the Earth in one hour and then humankind's energy use in a year, and record the energy of each in exajoules ($1\,\text{EJ} = 10^{18}\,\text{J}$). Compare the numbers with each other.

activities.title: An energy chain from a power plant to a kettle
activities.text:
An example chain (a calculated model, not a measurement): the chemical energy of the fuel turns into electricity in a power plant, the electricity travels through the grid to a home, and a kettle heats the water. The table shows the useful energy left at each step.

| Step | Energy | Form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fuel | $100\,\text{MJ}$ | chemical |
| Power plant | $40\,\text{MJ}$ | electricity |
| Grid | $38\,\text{MJ}$ | electricity |
| Water | $34\,\text{MJ}$ | thermal energy |

question.prompt: How many megajoules of the energy of the fuel have ended up somewhere other than the water along the chain? Answer in megajoules.
hints: Energy is conserved. How much energy was there at the start, and how much of it is in the water at the end?
The energy that did not end up in the water is the difference between the initial energy and the energy transferred to the water: $E_\text{other} = E_\text{start} - E_\text{water}$.

mistakes.feedback: You calculated only the heat of the power plant, $100\,\text{MJ} - 40\,\text{MJ}$. Energy also turns into heat in the grid and in the kettle, and the share of the whole chain is the difference between the initial energy and what remained in the water.
$34\,\text{MJ}$ is the energy transferred to the water, not the energy that went elsewhere. The question asks for the rest, when there was $100\,\text{MJ}$ at the start.

question.solution:
**Given:** chemical energy of the fuel $E_\text{start} = 100\,\text{MJ}$ and energy transferred to the water $E_\text{water} = 34\,\text{MJ}$

**Find:** energy that ended up somewhere other than the water $E_\text{other}$ in megajoules

**Principle:** Energy is conserved, so the initial energy is divided entirely between the water and elsewhere. The other energy is heat that was produced in the power plant, the grid and the kettle and spread into the surroundings.

**Formula:** $E_\text{start} = E_\text{water} + E_\text{other}$, so $E_\text{other} = E_\text{start} - E_\text{water}$

**Conversions:** Not needed: all energies are given in megajoules.

**Substitution:** $E_\text{other} = 100\,\text{MJ} - 34\,\text{MJ} = 66\,\text{MJ}$

**Answer:** $66\,\text{MJ}$, two significant figures as in the data $34\,\text{MJ}$.

**Reasonableness:** The heat at the steps is $100\,\text{MJ} - 40\,\text{MJ} = 60\,\text{MJ}$, $40\,\text{MJ} - 38\,\text{MJ} = 2\,\text{MJ}$ and $38\,\text{MJ} - 34\,\text{MJ} = 4\,\text{MJ}$, and together they make $60\,\text{MJ} + 2\,\text{MJ} + 4\,\text{MJ} = 66\,\text{MJ}$. This is more than the energy that remained in the water, as in power plants.

activities.title: Conclusion: how much energy is there and where does it go?
activities.prompt: Write, on the basis of your tables and the energy chain: which was greater, a litre of petrol or a day's food, and by what factor? How did the energy from the Sun in one hour compare with the energy use of humankind in a year? What form does the energy of the chain finally end up in?
activities.model: A litre of petrol was about $32\,\text{MJ}$ and a day's food about $10\,\text{MJ}$, so petrol contains about $32\,\text{MJ} : 10\,\text{MJ} \approx 3$ times as much energy. The solar radiation reaching the Earth in an hour and the energy use of humankind in a year were each about $620\,\text{EJ}$, that is, $6.2 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{J}$, in the table, so they are of the same order of magnitude. In an energy chain, energy is conserved, but a large part turns into heat at every step and spreads into the surroundings. The values are rounded orders of magnitude, partly estimates.
criteria: I compared petrol and food using numbers and said by what factor they differ.
I said that an hour of the Sun and a year of humankind are of the same order of magnitude.
I explained that the energy of the chain is conserved but ends up largely as heat.
I mentioned that the values are rounded orders of magnitude.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the tables. Then return to the opening question: where does the energy of the bicycle come from, and where does it go when you stop? Describe the chain step by step.

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A student converts the energy $2.5\,\text{kJ}$ to joules and writes $2.5\,\text{kJ} = 2.5 : 1000\,\text{J} = 0.0025\,\text{J}$. Where is the error?

choices.text: Kilo means a thousand, so the number should be multiplied by a thousand: $2.5 \cdot 1000\,\text{J} = 2500\,\text{J}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The prefix kilo means a thousand, so a kilojoule contains a thousand joules, and in joules the number is a thousand times larger. You can check the reasonableness from the order of magnitude: the joule is a smaller unit than the kilojoule, so the number must grow.

choices.text: There is no error, because a smaller unit means a smaller number.
choices.feedback: On the contrary: the joule is a smaller unit than the kilojoule, so the same energy needs more joules, that is, a larger number.

choices.text: The result should have been divided by a hundred as well, because kilo is a hundred.
choices.feedback: Kilo is a thousand, not a hundred. The conversion is done by replacing the prefix with its value, $\text{kJ} = 1000\,\text{J}$.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A wind farm produces electrical energy of $360\,\text{GJ}$ in a day. In the grid, $9\,\text{GJ}$ turns into heat on the way, and consumers use $0.300\,\text{TJ}$ of electricity. The rest is stored in a battery. How many gigajoules are stored in the battery?
hints: Where does all the electrical energy that was produced go? Energy does not disappear.
Write the conservation law: the energy produced equals the energy that turned into heat, the energy used by consumers and the stored energy, added together. Solve for the stored energy.
First convert to the same unit: $0.300\,\text{TJ} = 0.300 \cdot 1000\,\text{GJ}$. Then $E_\text{battery} = 360\,\text{GJ} - 9\,\text{GJ} - 300\,\text{GJ}$.

mistakes.feedback: The number $51\,000$ is the correct result in megajoules: $51\,000\,\text{MJ} = 51 \cdot 1000\,\text{MJ} = 51\,\text{GJ}$. The question asks for gigajoules, so give the answer in gigajoules.
You subtracted only the heat of the grid, $360\,\text{GJ} - 9\,\text{GJ}$. The energy used by consumers, $300\,\text{GJ}$, must also be subtracted to get the energy left for the battery.

activities.solution:
**Given:** electrical energy produced $E_\text{produced} = 360\,\text{GJ}$, heat in the grid $E_\text{heat} = 9\,\text{GJ}$, consumers $E_\text{use} = 0.300\,\text{TJ}$

**Find:** energy stored in the battery $E_\text{battery}$ in gigajoules

**Principle:** Energy is conserved: the energy produced is divided into heat, the consumers and the battery. Nothing disappears, so the parts together equal the energy produced.

**Formula:** $E_\text{produced} = E_\text{heat} + E_\text{use} + E_\text{battery}$, so $E_\text{battery} = E_\text{produced} - E_\text{heat} - E_\text{use}$

**Conversions:** Replace the terajoule with its value: $0.300\,\text{TJ} = 0.300 \cdot 1000\,\text{GJ} = 300\,\text{GJ}$.

**Substitution:** $E_\text{battery} = 360\,\text{GJ} - 9\,\text{GJ} - 300\,\text{GJ} = 51\,\text{GJ}$

**Answer:** $51\,\text{GJ}$, to the accuracy of a whole gigajoule: in a subtraction the least precise value decides the accuracy, and all the data ($360\,\text{GJ}$, $9\,\text{GJ}$ and $0.300\,\text{TJ} = 300\,\text{GJ}$) are known to the accuracy of a gigajoule.

**Reasonableness:** A small part of the energy produced is left for the battery, and the sum is correct: $9\,\text{GJ} + 300\,\text{GJ} + 51\,\text{GJ} = 360\,\text{GJ}$. The heat in the grid is the smallest item, which fits the fact that transmission losses are small.

activities.text: Practise at three levels. In Level 1 exercises you convert prefixes and use conservation of energy, Level 2 exercises also have a second step, and Level 3 requires reasoning.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: A battery has been charged with $54\,\text{kJ}$. A video is watched on a phone, and the battery runs flat. Which description of the energy of the battery is correct?

choices.text: The energy of the battery has run out, so it no longer exists.
choices.feedback: Energy does not run out. The chemical energy of the battery has turned into light, sound and heat, and in the end everything has spread as heat into the surroundings.

choices.text: The $54\,\text{kJ}$ of the battery has turned into other forms in the phone, finally almost entirely into heat, and there is as much energy in total as at the start.
choices.feedback: Correct. Chemical energy turns into electricity, light, sound and heat, and in the end everything ends up as heat in the surroundings. Energy is conserved.

choices.text: The energy of the battery has increased, because the phone gets warm.
choices.feedback: The phone getting warm is the energy of the battery turning into heat. Heat is not new energy; the chemical energy of the battery decreases by exactly as much as the thermal energy increases.

activities.title: 2. Comparison
activities.prompt: A lightning strike releases on average about $1.0\,\text{GJ}$ of energy, and the energy of a day's food is $10\,\text{MJ}$. How many days' food does the energy of a lightning strike correspond to?
hints: Both energies must be in the same unit so that they can be compared.
The number is the energy of the lightning divided by the energy of a day's food: $1000\,\text{MJ} : 10\,\text{MJ}$.

mistakes.feedback: You divided the numbers $1.0$ and $10$ without converting the units. A gigajoule is a thousand megajoules, so convert first: $1.0\,\text{GJ} = 1.0 \cdot 1000\,\text{MJ} = 1000\,\text{MJ}$, and then divide $1000\,\text{MJ} : 10\,\text{MJ}$.

You divided the energy of a day's food by the energy of the lightning and converted the units, $10\,\text{MJ} : 1000\,\text{MJ} = 0.01$. The ratio is the wrong way round: the question asks how many days' food the energy of the lightning corresponds to, so you divide the energy of the lightning by the energy of the food, $1000\,\text{MJ} : 10\,\text{MJ}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** lightning $E_\text{lightning} = 1.0\,\text{GJ}$ and a day's food $E_\text{food} = 10\,\text{MJ}$

**Find:** number of days' food $N$

**Principle:** The number is obtained by dividing the energy of the lightning by the energy of one day's food, when both are in the same unit.

**Formula:** $N = E_\text{lightning} : E_\text{food}$

**Conversions:** $1.0\,\text{GJ} = 1.0 \cdot 1000\,\text{MJ} = 1000\,\text{MJ}$

**Substitution:** $N = E_\text{lightning} : E_\text{food} = 1000\,\text{MJ} : 10\,\text{MJ} = 100$

**Answer:** About $100$ days' food, two significant figures as in the data $1.0\,\text{GJ}$ and $10\,\text{MJ}$.

**Reasonableness:** A gigajoule is a thousand megajoules and a day's food is ten, so the ratio is a thousand divided by ten, about a hundred. The energy of the lightning would last a person over three months, but the lightning releases it in a fraction of a second.

activities.title: 3. Explain and transfer
activities.prompt: Explain why we say that energy cannot be used up, even though a petrol tank becomes empty. Use driving a car as an example and use the words energy chain and thermal energy.
criteria: I say that energy does not disappear but changes form.
I describe the chain: chemical energy, motion, heat.
I say that in the end a large part is heat that spreads into the surroundings.
I explain why the heat can no longer easily be put to use.
activities.model: In the engine of a car, the chemical energy of petrol turns into motion and heat. When driving, air resistance, the tyres and the brakes turn the energy of the motion into thermal energy, which spreads into the air and the road. So no energy disappears: there is the same amount of energy at the start and at the end of the chain. The tank becomes empty because the energy has changed into a form that can no longer be collected back and used. That is why new energy is needed all the time, for example from fuel or from the Sun.

activities.text: Finally, three quick questions. Answer first on your own and open the answer only after that.
